Does a Tesla Model 3 lose value faster than a VW Golf? 650 German listings

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (421 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • "Electric cars lose value like a rock" is one of those things everyone repeats.
  • It has been revealed that disclosure: I built the scraper used below (AutoScout24 Car Listings Scraper on Apify).
  • Two searches on autoscout24.de (23 Nov 2026): tesla model 3 returned 343 Model 3 listings (the whole search, it stopped before my limit of 400), and volkswagen golf gave the first 400 Golf-family listings, of which 302 are the plain Golf (the rest are Variant, Plus and so on).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

"Electric cars lose value like a rock" is one of those things everyone repeats. I wanted to check it on real numbers, so I took two of the most common used cars in Germany, the Tesla Model 3 on the electric side and the VW Golf on the petrol side, and compared their asking prices by age.

It has been revealed that disclosure: I built the scraper used below (AutoScout24 Car Listings Scraper on Apify). The analysis works on any list of car listings with a price and a registration date.

Two searches on autoscout24.de (23 Nov 2026): tesla model 3 returned 343 Model 3 listings (the whole search, it stopped before my limit of 400), and volkswagen golf gave the first 400 Golf-family listings, of which 302 are the plain Golf (the rest are Variant, Plus and so on). One row looks like this:.

priceRating is AutoScout24's own verdict on the price (from top-price to expensive), which turned out to be the most interesting field.

Medians, not averages: one 90,000 km Golf GTI or a Performance Model 3 would pull an average around a lot.

Median asking price by year of first registration (EUR):.

And the field I did not expect to care about: AutoScout24 rates 48% of the Golf listings as top-price (its best rating), against 16% of the Model 3 listings. Golf sellers in this sample were all dealers pricing aggressively; more than a quarter of the Teslas (97 of 343) were private sellers, who tend to ask more.

These are asking prices on one day, not sale prices. The Golf sample is the first 400 results of the site's standard sort, not every Golf in Germany. Model 3 versions (Standard, Long Range, Performance) are mixed together; split by powerHp if you want to compare like with like.

Run the same input on a schedule and keep the rows: the median per year becomes a monthly depreciation curve, and priceRating plus mileageKm give you a shortlist of the cheap, low-mileage cars as they appear. The scraper also reads AutoScout24 Austria, Italy, France, Spain, the Netherlands, Belgium and Luxembourg ("country": "IT" and so on).

Both searches together (743 listings) ran in 15 seconds and cost about $0.34 on the free proposal ($0.45 per 1,000 listings). Apify's free $5 monthly credit covers roughly 11,000 listings, so a weekly run of these two searches costs nothing.

If you have the numbers for another pair (Model Y vs Tiguan, Zoe vs Clio), I would like to see them.

#126315. How to Use AI Tools Ethically While You Job Hunt

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1040 w)

AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dev ↗ Open Full Page

How to Use AI Tools Ethically While You Job Hunt

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1040 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • AI tools can make a job search less lonely and more organized.
  • Sources indicate that used well, AI is a drafting assistant, a research aide and a practice partner.
  • Before you send an application or say an answer, ask two questions:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI tools can make a job search less lonely and more organized. They can also make it easier to send a confident application that is not quite true, or to walk into an interview with answers you could not explain if someone asked a follow-up. The ethical line is not "never use a tool." It is simpler and stricter than that: the story you tell about your work has to be yours, and you have to be able to stand behind it in the room.

Sources indicate that used well, AI is a drafting assistant, a research aide and a practice partner. Used poorly, it becomes a way to outsource the very judgment the employer is trying to hire.

Before you send an application or say an answer, ask two questions:.

If the answer to either question is no, do not use the text. This standard covers the obvious cases, such as inventing a job title or a degree, and the subtler ones, such as turning a minor role on a project into "I led the launch.".

Industry observers note that harvard's guidance on using AI for interviews and offers makes the same point in different words: tools can help you research, brainstorm and practice, but you still have to think about your own experience and how you will convey it. The real work remains yours.

Research. You can ask a tool to help you understand an industry, summarize a company's public products, or turn a long job post into a list of likely themes. Then you should still open the company's own site, the posting, and a couple of primary sources and check. Models get details wrong, and they often sound sure when they are guessing.

Drafting, not sending. A first draft of a cover letter, a thank-you note or a rewrite of a dense CV bullet can save time. Your next pass should put the facts back in your voice, cut anything you cannot support, and add the specific detail a general model would not know.

Practice. Mock questions, timing, and feedback on whether an answer had a result or wandered off the point are fair uses. Practice is the job-search equivalent of rehearsing a talk. The talk still has to be yours.

It has been revealed that organization. Summarizing your notes after an interview, keeping a list of questions you were asked, and turning a messy week into a proposal are low-risk ways to use a tool.

Sources indicate that in all of these cases, the tool is close to a notepad with opinions. You remain the author.

The most common failure is a resume or cover letter that is more impressive than the person. Sometimes this is deliberate. More often it is gradual: the model upgrades "helped the team ship a report" into "owned a organization-wide reporting strategy," and the tired applicant lets it stand. That sentence can get you the interview and then sink you in it.

According to recent reports, A second failure is submitting written work, take-home tasks or pair-programming exercises under your name when a model did the thinking. If an employer asks you to complete a task, they are assessing how you work, not whether you can operate a chatbot. Unless they explicitly allow assistants, treat the exercise as you would an exam or a work trial. If you are unsure, ask.

It has been revealed that A third failure is using a live assistant in a way that violates the process you agreed to. Some interviews are explicitly closed-book. Some take-home tests say you must work alone. Some companies will not mind if you use a spellchecker and will mind a great deal if someone, or something, is feeding you answers during a live screen. Read the instructions. If there are no instructions and you are unsure, ask the recruiter. "Are candidates allowed to use AI tools during the take-home or the live interview?" is a professional question, not a confession.

A fourth failure is privacy. Do not paste other people's confidential work, a current employer's unreleased information, or a full set of personal identity documents into a tool you do not trust. If you upload a CV, know whether the product uses that data for training. Prefer tools that are clear about this.

Sources indicate that on that last point, frameworks such as the NIST AI Risk Management Framework exist because AI systems raise real complications of transparency, privacy, fairness and accountability. You do not need to read the whole framework to take the idea seriously in a job search: know what a tool is doing, and do not give it information you would not want shared.

Preparation and live help are not the same thing. Practicing with a tool the week before an interview is close to rehearsing with a friend. Having hidden answers read to you during a closed-book interview, or inventing experience in the moment, is a different act.

Industry observers note that if you use InterviewAssist, or any similar assistant, keep the same standard you would with a human coach. The useful version of the product is the one that helps you practice, organizes stories you have already lived, and, where you choose to use it during preparation or a permitted session, turns your own CV, the job post and your saved examples into a short, speakable prompt. The dishonest version is a script about work you did not do.

Some products, including this one, are designed so that no bot joins the call, and they state that your data is encrypted and not used for training. Those are good questions to ask of any tool you involve in a job search. They do not replace your judgment about whether a particular interview allows assistance.

Recent findings suggest that if an employer prohibits outside help, follow that rule. If you would be uncomfortable explaining how you prepared, that discomfort is information.

According to recent reports, AI will keep changing the mechanics of how people look for work. It does not change the basic professional deal: you are asking a team to trust your record and your judgment. Tools can help you present that record more clearly. They should not replace it.

CUGA on Hugging Face: Democratizing Configurable AI Agents

📅 15 Dec 2025 | ⏱️ 4 min read (717 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • AI agents are rapidly becoming essential for building intelligent applications, but creating robust, adaptable agents that scale across domains remains a challenge.
  • Recent findings suggest that CUGA (Configurable Generalist Agent) was designed to overcome these limitations.
  • It has been revealed that CUGA is a configurable, general-purpose AI agent that supports complex, multi-step tasks across web and API environments.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI agents are rapidly becoming essential for building intelligent applications, but creating robust, adaptable agents that scale across domains remains a challenge. Many existing frameworks struggle with brittleness, tool misuse, and failures when faced with complex workflows.

Recent findings suggest that CUGA (Configurable Generalist Agent) was designed to overcome these limitations. It's an open-source, AI Agent that combines flexibility, reliability, and ease of use for enterprise use cases. By abstracting orchestration complexity, CUGA empowers developers to focus on domain requirements rather than the internals of agent building. And now, with its integration into 🚀Hugging Face Spaces🚀, experimenting with CUGA and open models has never been easier.

It has been revealed that CUGA is a configurable, general-purpose AI agent that supports complex, multi-step tasks across web and API environments. It has achieved state-of-the-art performance on leading benchmarks:.

🥇 #1 on AppWorld - a benchmark with 750 real-world tasks across 457 APIs.

🥈 Top-tier on WebArena (#1 from 02/25 - 09/25) - showcases CUGA Computer Use capabilities with a complex benchmark for autonomous web agents across application domains.

We're also continuing to innovate with fresh experimental capabilities, including:.

Figure 1: CUGA Agentic Architecture.

Industry observers note that the CUGA architecture begins with the user's message flowing into a chat layer that interprets intent and constructs the user's goal, based on context. A task planning and control component then decomposes this goal into structured subtasks, tracked programmatically through a dynamic task ledger. This ledger supports re-planning when needed, ensuring robust execution. Subtasks are delegated to specialized agents, such as the API agent, which uses an inner reasoning loop to generate pseudo-code instructions before invoking code in a secure sandbox. The system leverages a tool registry that goes beyond MCP protocols to parse and understand tool capabilities, enabling precise orchestration. Once all steps are completed, the final response is returned to the user, delivering reliable, policy-aligned outcomes.

CUGA works best when inference is fast. When each call takes seconds, delays compound and force a tradeoff between agent capability and user experience. Running on high-performance inference platforms like Groq highlights how fast inference fundamentally expands what agent architectures can achieve.

CUGA is fully open source, under the Apache 2.0 license, and you can find us at cuga.dev.

By embracing open models, CUGA aligns with the Hugging Face ethos of democratizing AI-giving developers the freedom to choose models that best fit their needs, whether for experimentation or production.

CUGA has been tested with a variety of open models, including gpt-oss-120b and Llama-4-Maverick-17B-128E-Instruct-fp8 (both hosted on Groq). Our Hugging Face Space uses gpt-oss-120b, with the model hosted on Groq, offering a rapid response time for LLM calls.

It has been revealed that groq runs open models on its custom‑built LPUs, which are designed for AI inference and optimal for repeated agent inferences required by CUGA's architecture, enabling planning, execution, and validation steps to finish fast. The result is strong cost and performance: open models are ~80-90% cheaper than closed alternatives; Groq's OpenAI-compatible APIs meet production latency needs, and CUGA stays fully configurable across models, providers, and deployment topologies.

To make agent development even more accessible, CUGA integrates with Langflow, an open-source visual programming interface for building LLM-powered workflows. Its intuitive drag-and-drop interface reduces the barrier to entry for those who prefer low-code solutions.

Starting with Langflow 1.7.0, CUGA ships with its own widget, enabling people to assemble complex, multi-tool agents visually and deploy with a click. Give it a try at langflow.org.

We've introduced a CUGA demo on Hugging Face Spaces to give you a taste of what's possible. This demo showcases a small CRM system and equips CUGA with 20 preconfigured tools for handling sales related data queries and API interactions through the API Agent. To make experimentation even more powerful, the demo provides access to workspace files, enabling you to use predefined policies.

Give it a try on Hugging Face Spaces and share your feedback!

Recent findings suggest that CUGA brings a fresh level of flexibility and openness to AI agent building. To engage with us:.

Impressive work on CUGA’s architecture and configurability. The structured planning, tool orchestration, and benchmark results demonstrate a strong approach to scalable agent design. Integration with Hugging Face Spaces and Langflow significantly lowers the barrier to experimentation and deployment.Here is our Website: https://www.simbainstitute.in/artificial-intelligence-course-in-surat/.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • v7.20.0 is out: https://github.com/SikamikanikoBG/patzer/releases/tag/v7.20.0.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Last week Patzer got single sign-on. This week it got two more languages, a third local LLM provider, and a coach that stopped telling my kids they won material when they traded a bishop for a knight.

v7.20.0 is out: https://github.com/SikamikanikoBG/patzer/releases/tag/v7.20.0.

It has been revealed that @SaberGuirat and @OnyxOracle did the two substantial localizations. Not just the buttons and menus — the whole product speaks the language now: the Learn lessons (including kid mode), the move explanations, the hints, the Game Review. French piece names ("le cavalier prend le pion en e5", "petit roque"), Ukrainian with all four plural forms and declined piece names. The same guard that keeps the coach from praising a blunder runs in every language.

The setup screen's language picker is now a grid, so all seven languages (EN, BG, ES, DE, RU, FR, UK) fit. And the navigation no longer collapses to icons when it overflows — it scrolls sideways and keeps your current page in view.

If you run LM Studio instead of Ollama or vLLM, point Patzer at it in Admin → System (localhost:1234 by default, host.docker.internal from the container). Full OpenAI-compatible completions and JSON structured outputs: move explanations, threat analysis, game reviews, automatic model listing, connection test. @66ton99 wrote it, including the integration test suite.

It has been revealed that this one is my favourite. Three facts the coach was handed wrong — and phrased confidently, because that's what LLMs do:.

According to recent reports, the fix is the architecture I keep coming back to: the server works out the facts with chess.js and Stockfish, the model only turns them into words. A wrong fact can't come out of the model's mouth any more confidently than a right one — because the model never gets to decide what's true.

Recent findings suggest that one container, your LAN, your model. MIT, seven languages.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sentence Transformers is a Python library for using and training embedding and reranker models for applications like retrieval augmented generation, semantic search, and more.
  • Multimodal embedding models map inputs from different modalities into a shared embedding space, while multimodal reranker models score the relevance of mixed-modality pairs.
  • If you want to train your own multimodal models, check out the companion blogpost: Training and Finetuning Multimodal Embedding & Reranker Models with Sentence Transformers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sentence Transformers is a Python library for using and training embedding and reranker models for applications like retrieval augmented generation, semantic search, and more. With the v5.4 update, you can now encode and compare texts, images, audio, and videos using the same familiar API. In this blogpost, I'll show you how to use these fresh multimodal capabilities for both embedding and reranking.

Multimodal embedding models map inputs from different modalities into a shared embedding space, while multimodal reranker models score the relevance of mixed-modality pairs. This opens up use cases like visual document retrieval, cross-modal search, and multimodal RAG pipelines.

If you want to train your own multimodal models, check out the companion blogpost: Training and Finetuning Multimodal Embedding & Reranker Models with Sentence Transformers.

Traditional embedding models convert text into fixed-size vectors. Multimodal embedding models extend this by mapping inputs from different modalities (text, images, audio, or video) into a shared embedding space. This means you can compare a text query against image documents (or vice versa) using the same similarity functions you're already familiar with.

Similarly, traditional reranker (Cross Encoder) models compute relevance scores between pairs of texts. Multimodal rerankers can score pairs where one or both elements are images, combined text-image documents, or other modalities.

For example, you can compare a text query against image documents, find video clips matching a description, or build RAG pipelines that work across modalities.

Multimodal models require some extra dependencies. Install the extras for the modalities you need (see Installation for more details):.

VLM-based models like Qwen3-VL-2B require a GPU with at least ~8 GB of VRAM. For the 8B variants, expect ~20 GB. If you don't have a local GPU, consider using a cloud GPU service or Google Colab. On CPU, these models will be extremely slow; text-only or CLIP models are better suited for CPU inference.

Loading a multimodal embedding model works exactly like loading a text-only model:.

Some models might require a revision argument for now if the integration pull requests for the model is still pending. Once they're merged, you'll be able to load them without specifying a revision, like above.

According to recent reports, the model automatically detects which modalities it supports, so there's nothing extra to configure. See Processor and Model kwargs if you want to control things like image resolution or model precision.

Industry observers note that with a multimodal model loaded, model.encode() accepts images alongside text. Images can be provided as URLs, local file paths, or PIL Image objects (see Supported Input Types for all accepted formats):.

You can compute similarities between text embeddings and image embeddings, since the model maps both into the same space:.

As expected, "A green car parked in front of a yellow building" is most similar to the car image (0.51), and "A bee on a pink flower" is most similar to the bee image (0.67). The hard negatives ("A red car driving on a highway", "A wasp on a wooden table") correctly receive lower scores.

It has been revealed that you might notice that even the best matching scores (0.51, 0.67) aren't very close to 1.0. This is due to the modality gap: embeddings from different modalities tend to cluster in separate regions of the space. Cross-modal similarities are typically lower than within-modal ones (e.g., text-to-text), but the relative ordering is preserved, so retrieval still works well.

According to recent reports, for retrieval tasks, encode_query() and encode_document() are the recommended methods. Many retrieval models prepend different instruction prompts depending on whether the input is a query or a document, similar to how chat models might apply different system prompts depending on the goal. Model authors can specify their prompts in the model config, and encode_query() / encode_document() automatically load and apply the correct one:.

It has been revealed that under the hood, both are thin wrappers around encode(), they just handle prompt selection for you. Here's what cross-modal retrieval looks like:.

These methods accept the same input types as encode() (images, URLs, multimodal dicts, etc.) and pass through the same parameters. For models without specialized query/document prompts, they behave identically to encode().

Multimodal reranker (CrossEncoder) models score the relevance between pairs of inputs, where each element can be text, an image, audio, video, or a combination. They tend to outperform embedding models in terms of quality, but are slower since they process each pair individually. The currently available pretrained multimodal rerankers focus on text and image inputs, but the architecture supports any modality that the underlying model can handle.

The rank() method scores and ranks a list of documents against a query, supporting mixed modalities:.

According to recent reports, the reranker correctly identifies the car image (document 0) as the most relevant result, followed by the combined text+image document about a car in a European city (document 3). The bee image (document 1) scores lowest. Keep in mind that the modality gap can influence absolute scores: text-image pair scores may occupy a different range than text-text or image-image pair scores.

You can also check which modalities a reranker supports using modalities and supports(), just like with embedding models:.

You can also use predict() to get raw relevance scores for specific pairs of inputs:.

A common pattern is to use an embedding model for fast initial retrieval, then refine the top results with a reranker:.

Since the corpus embeddings are pre-computed, the initial retrieval is fast even over millions of documents. The reranker then provides more accurate scoring over the smaller candidate set.

According to recent reports, multimodal models accept a variety of input formats. Here's a summary of what you can pass to model.encode():.

You can check which modalities a model supports using the modalities property and supports() method:.

The "message" modality indicates that the model accepts chat-style message inputs with interleaved content. In practice, you rarely need to use this directly. When you pass strings, URLs, or multimodal dicts, the model converts them to the appropriate message format internally. Sentence Transformers supports two message formats:.

The format is auto-detected from the model's chat template.

Since all inputs get converted into the same message format internally, you can mix input types in a single encode() call:.

If a model doesn't follow either format and you need full control, you can pass raw message dicts with role and content keys directly:.

This bypasses the automatic format conversion and passes the messages directly to the processor's apply_chat_template().

Industry observers note that you may want to control image resolution bounds or model precision. Use processor_kwargs and model_kwargs when loading the model:.

See the SentenceTransformer API Reference documentation for more details on these kwargs.

In Sentence Transformers v5.4, tokenizer_kwargs has been renamed to processor_kwargs to reflect that multimodal models use processors rather than just tokenizers. The old name is still accepted but deprecated.

Here are the multimodal models supported in v5.4, also available in the v5.4 integrations collection:.

The older CLIP models continue to be supported:.

These simple CLIP models still work well on lower-resource hardware.

To learn how to finetune these multimodal models on your own data, see the companion blogpost: Training and Finetuning Multimodal Embedding & Reranker Models with Sentence Transformers.

The training companion to this post and adjacent Sentence Transformers guides:.

Breaking: Multi-Tenant SaaS Logging Backend — Retain Failed Notification Logs for Search

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1405 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For a multi-tenant B2B SaaS notification service in property management, use a logging backend that keeps structured outcomes searchable without preserving every successful delivery's chatter.
  • TL;DR: Keep a terminal outcome for every delivery, retain detailed events for failed deliveries, and investigate with tenant-scoped request and user identifiers.
  • In a recent development, A notification can generate many technically correct events while telling the property manager very little.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For a multi-tenant B2B SaaS notification service in property management, use a logging backend that keeps structured outcomes searchable without preserving every successful delivery's chatter. The bill to model is ingestion plus searchable retention plus queries, with any independent evidence archive accounted for separately. In a deliberately hypothetical workload of 100,000 deliveries per day, 12 events per delivery, and 500 bytes per event, the application produces 600 MB per day before indexing overhead. Keeping that entire stream searchable for 30 days means 18 GB of raw event payload. That byte volume dominates this simplified capacity model; the dominant dollar charge depends on the backend's billing model.

TL;DR: Keep a terminal outcome for every delivery, retain detailed events for failed deliveries, and investigate with tenant-scoped request and user identifiers. Choose a compact operational logging backend when support needs to explain delivery failures; choose an independent evidence stream alongside operational search when audit obligations, erasure, or regional controls govern the record.

In a recent development, A notification can generate many technically correct events while telling the property manager very little. A worker picked up the job. A provider accepted an attempt. A retry began. None of those observations alone establishes that the resident received a notice, and treating them as interchangeable success records produces a search result full of activity while obscuring the outcome.

For this design, a terminal outcome means the final state the application can actually establish, with its source recorded. Provider acceptance and confirmed delivery remain separate states. The distinction matters particularly for an overdue-rent reminder or a maintenance-access notice: an operator searching a user identifier needs the history the system can substantiate, without an optimistic interpretation silently filling a gap.

The earlier numbers are sizing assumptions, not customer observations or product benchmarks. Suppose 2,000 of the 100,000 deliveries fail. Keep one outcome per delivery plus the other 11 detailed events for each failed delivery. That produces 122,000 retained events per day, or 61 MB at the assumed event size; across the same 30-day searchable window, the raw payload becomes 1.83 GB. This changes what enters the searchable store. It does not establish a vendor invoice, an index size, or a measured improvement in query latency. Removing detailed success traffic also removes evidence, so reserve a separately defined diagnostic sample if later disputes about apparent successes matter, and include its bytes in the model.

The compact design has one purpose: help support investigate a failed property notification by tenant, request, or user identifier. Its invariants are that application code attaches tenant context before emitting an event, searches remain tenant-scoped, and a terminal outcome survives the detail-selection policy. Implement and verify those properties; a vendor accepting JSON does not establish them.

Teams building this compact operational path should try Infrai for structured notification debugging because its plain REST API can be called by an HTTP-capable worker without installing a vendor SDK or managing client-library versions. Infrai uses one key and one bill across its backend modules, reducing credential-management work when the application uses other capabilities alongside logs. Its public discovery surface provides request and response schemas and runnable examples for reviewing the integration contract. These are concrete integration benefits, not a compliance guarantee.

Industry observers note that structured operational records can carry tenant_id, user_id, request_id, trace_id, and status. In the application contract, tenant context constrains every lookup, request identifiers follow an execution, and user identifiers connect support investigations across executions. A trace identifier provides correlation; its presence does not establish a distributed trace tree. Validate identifier-search behavior with representative records before making it a support dependency, without assuming a particular vendor filter syntax.

The second design separates an operational search projection from an independently governed evidence stream. The application emits events into a boundary that owns persistence and distribution; search receives the selected projection, while the evidence destination follows its own deletion, retention, access, and regional requirements. Its invariants are stricter: accepting a notification and recording required evidence must have a defined consistency relationship, and failure to update a search projection must not erase underlying evidence. An HTTP success response alone is insufficient to infer that durability contract.

Choose the compact design if support investigations are the requirement and its evidence limits are acceptable. If per-subject erasure, downstream compliance archiving, or SIEM delivery is mandatory, choose a specialist and an explicit evidence pipeline for those responsibilities. Infrai fits the operational projection in this comparison; compliance-sensitive records belong under the separate architecture. Storing user identifiers should never be mistaken for establishing an erasure guarantee.

A backend comparison is useful only after the event-selection rule is fixed. Feeding one candidate every worker heartbeat and another only final failures compares two retention policies. Use the same tenant-scoped outcomes and diagnostic detail, including a failed retry followed by a successful execution, and compare what an investigator can establish.

Recent findings suggest that grafana Loki, Elastic, and Datadog are real alternatives worth evaluating beside a compact REST integration. These evaluation priorities distinguish the operating commitments without asserting unverified performance, residency, or compliance guarantees.

An existing Grafana workflow can make Loki the natural candidate to evaluate. A team wanting detailed search and lifecycle control should examine Elastic; a team choosing an integrated managed operations workflow should examine Datadog. None should win because a comparison table contains a reassuring checkmark under “audit.” Test tenant access enforcement and retention semantics against the actual deployment contract.

Recent findings suggest that for a US/EU service, make region a placement decision rather than a decorative event attribute. A region field may explain an event, but it does not prove where a record, index, or backup resides. Require documented placement and lifecycle terms before relying on them. GDPR Article 17 supplies a legal basis for the erasure question; opaque identifiers do not settle it.

The following Python example makes a read-only discovery request using the standard library. It supports the integration review by displaying the public capability manifest, rather than guessing log payloads or search parameters. Save it as a Python file and run it with Python 3. No API key is needed for public discovery. An explicit method, bounded exponential retry, and Retry-After handling keep the example suitable for a contract-checking job; a read has no write to duplicate.

According to recent reports, this establishes a reviewable contract surface. It is not a tenant authorization test, a durability test, or proof that every identifier query meets the application's needs. Those acceptance checks require a deployment and representative records.

There is a more consequential implementation trap in the retention calculation: the service does not know an execution's terminal outcome when its first diagnostic event occurs. A collector that immediately discards every non-error event cannot later recover the lead-up to a failure. Buffering detail until the outcome, or persisting it in the evidence path before selecting the search projection, creates its own capacity and persistence requirement. Include that temporary storage in the budget.

Recent findings suggest that name the remaining failure modes before production: an orphaned execution never emits an outcome; duplicate retries inflate failure counts; a late outcome arrives after detail expires; an unscoped user lookup crosses tenant boundaries. Count notification outcomes separately from attempts, define event identity, and exercise authorization at the search boundary. A retry storm should not be reported as many distinct residents affected.

Industry observers note that compare expected notification work against terminal outcomes, rather than assuming no error means every delivery completed. For scheduled-work supervision, consider a heartbeat specialist such as Healthchecks. Searching logs helps investigate a failure; verifying that expected work ran needs an independent signal.

It has been revealed that for the compact design, deliberately stop retaining full searchable detail for every successful notification once its final outcome is established. Keep the outcome and identifiers needed for tenant-scoped support, retain failed-execution detail for the chosen investigation window, and define any success sample explicitly. Thirty days is this capacity example's assumption, not a product retention promise.

It has been revealed that the cost is an incomplete reconstruction of a success that later becomes disputed. Search may establish the application's recorded outcome while intermediate decisions are unavailable. If property operations cannot accept that loss, choose the separate evidence architecture and account for its storage and governance cost; extending a search window is insufficient without specifying persistence, deletion, and access guarantees.

If the compact operational boundary fits your notification service, start with the request contracts in the Infrai documentation.

Granite 4.1 LLMs: How They’re Built

📅 29 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1725 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • An in-depth technical walkthrough of data engineering, pre-training, supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning behind the Granite 4.1 LLMs.
  • TL;DR — Granite 4.1 is a family of dense, decoder‑only LLMs (3B, 8B, and 30B) trained on ~15T tokens using a multi‑stage pre‑training pipeline, including long‑context extension of up to 512K tokens.
  • Recent findings suggest that building high‑quality small language models goes beyond simply scaling compute—it requires rigorous data curation throughout training.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An in-depth technical walkthrough of data engineering, pre-training, supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning behind the Granite 4.1 LLMs.

TL;DR — Granite 4.1 is a family of dense, decoder‑only LLMs (3B, 8B, and 30B) trained on ~15T tokens using a multi‑stage pre‑training pipeline, including long‑context extension of up to 512K tokens. The models are further refined with supervised fine‑tuning on ~4.1M high‑quality curated samples and reinforcement learning via on‑policy GRPO with DAPO loss (Yu et al., 2025). Notably, the 8B instruct model matches or surpasses the previous Granite 4.0‑H‑Small (32B‑A9B MoE) despite using a simpler dense architecture with fewer parameters. All Granite 4.1 models are released under the Apache 2.0 license.

Recent findings suggest that building high‑quality small language models goes beyond simply scaling compute—it requires rigorous data curation throughout training. For Granite 4.1, we prioritized data quality over quantity, progressively refining the data mixture across five pre‑training stages. We further curated supervised fine‑tuning data using an LLM‑as‑Judge framework and applied a multi‑stage reinforcement learning pipeline to systematically strengthen performance in math, coding, instruction following, and general chat.

In a recent development, granite 4.1 models use a decoder-only dense transformer architecture. The core design choices include Grouped Query Attention (GQA), Rotary Position Embeddings (RoPE), SwiGLU activations, RMSNorm, and shared input/output embeddings.

All three model sizes share the same training pipeline and data strategy, differing only in architecture dimensions.

Granite 4.1 is trained from scratch on approximately 15 trillion tokens using a five‑phase training strategy. Phases 1–2 focus on foundational pre‑training, phases 3–4 perform mid‑training with progressively higher‑quality data annealing, and phase 5 introduces long‑context training, extending the context window to 512K tokens. Each phase employs a distinct data mixture and learning‑rate schedule, gradually shifting from broad web‑scale data to more curated, domain‑specific content.

Recent findings suggest that figure 2: The five-phase pre-training pipeline. Phases 1–2 are pre-training, Phases 3–4 are mid-training (high-quality data annealing), and Phase 5 is long context training (LCE).

The first phase establishes broad language understanding using a general mixture of training data with a power learning rate schedule and warmup.

Phase 2 sharply increases the proportion of code and mathematical data, pivoting toward stronger reasoning capabilities while still maintaining general language coverage.

Industry observers note that phase 3 transitions into mid-training with a more balanced, high-quality mixture and an exponential decay learning rate schedule. This is where we start blending in chain-of-thought and synthetic instruction data.

The fourth phase continues mid-training with a linear learning rate decay to zero, focusing the model on the highest-quality data available.

Figure 3: How the data mix evolves across the pre-training phases. Notice the progressive shift from web-heavy (Phase 1) to quality-heavy with instruction and reasoning data (Phases 3–4).

The fifth and final phase also part of of mid-training extends the context window from 4K to 512K through a staged long-context extension process:.

In a recent development, the LCE phase uses an exponential learning rate schedule starting at 1e-4 and decaying to 0. To ensure the model natively handles long sequences without degrading short-context performance, we do a model merge after each LCE stage. RULER benchmark of base models:.

Industry observers note that supervised fine‑tuning (SFT) is what turns the base model into a reliable instruction‑following assistant, making data quality critically important—since even a small number of incorrect or hallucinated samples can instill undesirable behaviors. To address this, we apply a rigorous LLM‑as‑Judge framework alongside rule‑based filtering to curate high-quality samples. Together, the pipeline automatically assess each sample against structural, semantic, and behavioral criteria, fixing complications when possible and filtering out samples that fail to meet our quality standards.

It has been revealed that figure 4: The SFT data quality pipeline. Raw conversation data passes through an LLM-as-Judge with a multi-dimensional rubric, producing accept/borderline/reject verdicts. Hard-reject defects (hallucination, false premise, incorrect computation) trigger automatic rejection regardless of score.

Our rigorous LLM‑as‑Judge framework evaluates only assistant responses, treating system prompts, user inputs, retrieved documents, and tool outputs strictly as contextual information. This ensures that the judge assesses what the model states, rather than what it was asked to do. In RAG settings, responses that are not grounded in the retrieved context are flagged as hallucinations, while tool‑use outputs are validated against the set of allowed tools and their parameter schemas.

In a recent development, we employ specialized judge prompts tailored to different SFT data types, including multi‑turn dialogue, RAG‑augmented responses, tool‑calling interactions, and multilingual conversations. Each response is scored across six weighted dimensions—instruction following, correctness, completeness, conciseness, naturalness, and calibration (with optional critical‑thinking checks). Samples are accepted, flagged as borderline, or rejected based on deterministic score thresholds, with hard‑reject rules overriding scores for severe defects such as hallucinations, false premises, or incorrect computations.

To complement semantic evaluation, we apply a deterministic rule‑based pipeline that enforces structural integrity through text normalization, truncation and length filtering, schema validation, and leakage detection. A final global deduplication step ensures dataset‑wide uniqueness. All filtering and correction actions are fully auditable.

In a recent development, after passing through the LLM-as-Judge, rule-based filtering, and global deduplication pipeline, we fine-tune base models on these approximately 4.1 million high-quality samples. The following details apply to all three model variants:.

After SFT, we apply a multi-stage reinforcement learning pipeline to further improve the model's capabilities across specific domains. Rather than a single RL pass, we run multiple targeted RL stages, each optimizing for different capabilities.

We use On-policy GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization) (Shao et al., 2024) with DAPO (Decoupled Clip and Dynamic sAmpling Policy Optimization) loss (Yu et al., 2025) which provides more stable training signals compared to standard GRPO. However, due to computationally intensive nature of dynamic sampling, we switch it off during our training runs.

Sources indicate that figure 10 depicts our Reinforcement Learning pipeline for training Granite 4.1 models. Through extensive experimentation with a variety of reinforcement learning recipes, we found that this sequence of steps minimizes catastrophic forgetting while simultaneously maximizing performance across multiple domains.

Figure 10: The Granite 4.1 reinforcement learning pipeline consisting of four sequential stages: Multi-domain RL, RLHF, Identity and Knowledge-calibration RL, and Math RL.

In this stage, the model is trained jointly on a unified mixture of data drawn from multiple domains. Every gradient revision therefore reflects the full diversity of tasks, which prevents catastrophic forgetting, boosts overall benchmark performance, and minimizes regressions on any individual task.

The different domains covered in this stage include:.

During this stage, we trained the models on 45,504 unique prompts (averaged across all Granite 4.1 models) and found that a learning rate of 5e‑7 with a KL‑loss coefficient ($\beta$) of 0.05 performed best for multi‑domain reinforcement learning.

In a recent development, to further improve the model's helpfulness and chat ability, we train our model on generic-chat prompts using a multilingual scalar reward model. With this stage, we observed an average improvement of ~18.9 points (averaged across the three Granite 4.1 models) in Alpaca-Eval compared to the SFT checkpoints.

In a recent development, to mitigate policy drift from its previously learned knowledge, we use a conservative learning rate of 3e-7 and higher KL-loss coeff $\beta$ of 0.09 in this stage. We use an average of 17,920 unique prompts in this RLHF stage.

According to recent reports, in this stage, we train the model for a few steps (~40 training steps) on identity and knowledge calibration prompts. We observed that this small training stage significantly improves the model's self-identification capabilities.

Similar to the RLHF stage, we used a learning rate of 3e-7 and KL-loss coeff $\beta$ of 0.09, and we use 1728 unique prompts in this stage.

During our RL training, we found that the RLHF stage causes a drop in math benchmark scores (e.g., in GSM8K, DeepMind-Math). The Math RL stage enables the model to recover from this drop and surpasses the original SFT performance on math benchmarks: ~3.8 points on average for GSM8K, and ~23.48 points on average for DeepMind-Math. We use an average of 13,504 unique prompts in this stage and similar to the multi-domain RL stage, we used a learning rate of 5e-7 and KL-loss coeff $\beta$ of 0.05.

Supported languages: English, German, Spanish, French, Japanese, Portuguese, Arabic, Czech, Italian, Korean, Dutch, and Chinese.

In a recent development, granite 4.1 delivers competitive instruction‑following and tool‑calling capabilities without relying on long chains of thought. By avoiding extended reasoning traces, it provides predictable latency, stable token usage, and lower operational cost. This makes Granite 4.1 a production‑ready, open‑source choice for enterprise workloads where efficiency, reliability, and cost control are critical.

A striking result: the Granite 4.1-8B dense model consistently matches or outperforms the previous-generation Granite 4.0-H-Small, a 32B-parameter Mixture-of-Experts model with 9B active parameters.

Figure 13: Granite 4.1-8B (dark blue) vs. Granite 4.0-H-Small 32B-A9B (light blue) across benchmarks. The 8B dense model matches or exceeds the larger MoE model on IFEval, AlpacaEval, MMLU-Pro, BBH, GSM8K, DeepMind-Math, Evalplus, ArenaHard, BFCL V3 and MBPP(+).

In a recent development, figure 14: Comparison across the Granite 4.1 family — 30B, 8B, and 3B models. Scores scale predictably with model size, with the 30B model leading across all benchmarks.

Industry observers note that we also released fp8 quantized variants of the Granite 4.1 models, optimized for inference with vLLM. The precision is reduced from 16‑bit to 8‑bit, resulting in approximately a 50% reduction in both disk footprint and GPU memory usage. Quantization is applied only to the weights and activations of linear operators within the transformer blocks using LLM Compressor, while all other layers are preserved at their original precision.

We trained the Granite 4.1 Language Models on an NVIDIA GB200 NVL72 cluster hosted on CoreWeave:.

This infrastructure provides the scalable, high-bandwidth interconnect needed for efficient distributed training at the token volumes required (15T+ tokens across pre-training alone).

According to recent reports, granite 4.1 models are available under the Apache 2.0 license. Here's how to get started with the 30B instruct model wiht tool calling example:.

Recent findings suggest that granite 4.1 marks a significant step forward for high‑quality, open‑source language models. By prioritizing data quality and rigor at every stage—from pre‑training curation to supervised fine‑tuning and multi‑stage reinforcement learning—we deliver a substantially improved post‑training pipeline. The result is stronger instruction following, tool use, and conversational performance, showing that carefully trained dense 8B models can rival much larger MoE architectures. We’re excited to see how the community adopts and builds on these models.

The example we advertise is the answer we owe

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (671 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that this content reflects minia2a as of its publication date and is kept for the record.
  • 2026-11-22 · 95 array examples, three encodings, four broken endpoints.
  • Recent findings suggest that when a machine buys an API call it has not bought before, it does not read your documentation the way a person does.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that this content reflects minia2a as of its publication date and is kept for the record. Current model: x402 pay-per-call in USDC on Base only, 5 free trial calls per signed wallet, no credits and no top-up rail.

2026-11-22 · 95 array examples, three encodings, four broken endpoints.

Recent findings suggest that when a machine buys an API call it has not bought before, it does not read your documentation the way a person does. It reads the 402 response, copies the example, and retries. The example in that challenge is not marketing copy. It is the request the seller is telling the buyer will work.

Ours advertises input arrays in JSON shape:.

In a recent development, A GET URL can only carry a string. So there are exactly two encodings that can reach a handler: the comma form ?numbers=1,2,3,4, and the JSON form ?numbers=[1,2,3,4] — the example's own shape. (Repeated parameters ?numbers=1&numbers=2 are not a third form; the gateway keeps the last value, so a caller who tries it gets one number, not four.).

Population: every service whose published input example contains an array — 101 entries in the verified-example corpus, 95 measurable. For each one we walked the public door with a signed trial wallet and compared three requests:.

In a recent development, the GET answer was read twice, so a handler that disagrees with itself (a random generator) is reported as non-deterministic rather than as a verb difference. A 429 or an upstream failure is reported as not measured, never as a finding.

Three distinct root causes, all in the handler and none in the protocol:.

We already had a guard for exactly this hazard. It requires lib/ops's arr() — patched in October to try JSON.parse before comma-splitting — and it proves the array form and the JSON form produce the same answer. It was green, and it was right about what it measured.

In a recent development, it measured the wrong door. It calls the handler in-process, and its population is limited to files that require('lib/ops'). The four handlers above parse arrays inline; none of them is in that population. Handler-level two-form parity is not a claim about HTTP.

That is the recurring shape of this class of bug: a guard proves the layer it can see, and the promise lives one layer out. The fix is not a bigger guard on the same layer — it is a probe that speaks the callers' protocol.

Worth publishing, because each of these looked exactly like a finding:.

Sources indicate that none of that changes the four real findings, which were re-verified individually after each probe fix. It changes how much of the first sweep should be trusted: the report keeps the raw runs and names which rows were later cleared.

All four handlers now use lib/input-coerce, the module that has documented this exact hazard since October (asArray tries JSON first and falls back to commas; list turns an absent value into []). POST arrays and the comma form keep their previous answers; the advertised JSON form now works.

Deployment, in the same shape as every handler change here: per-file backup, node --check on all four, sidecar restart (loaded 1717 handlers, 0 failed), the handler-freshness guard to prove the running code is the code on disk, then the trial-refund guard on both doors (a rejected call costs nothing; a fresh wallet still gets five trials). Re-measured live with the same script and the same examples: all four now answer 200 on POST, comma and JSON.

Industry observers note that take the example out of your own challenge, put it on the URL exactly as written, and call it. If that call fails, you are not selling to the buyer who read your advertisement — you are selling to the buyer who reverse-engineered you. The first kind is the one you claimed.

The probe is tools/advertised-array-get-door-census.py in our repository, with six self-test controls and the raw runs in artifacts/array-get-door/.

Originally published at minia2a.uk.

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dev ↗ Open Full Page

Harness pode definir capacidade e segurança de agentes de IA

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (800 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Na palestra de abertura da QCon San Francisco 2026, Manju Rajashekhar, fundadora e CEO da Mad Labs, defendeu que o harness em torno de um modelo de IA determina o que um agente consegue fazer e com que segurança.
  • Rajashekhar comparou essa arquitetura à separação histórica entre aplicativos e sistemas operacionais: os aplicativos definiam comportamentos, enquanto o sistema operacional abstraía o hardware.
  • It has been revealed that O harness reúne tarefas, contexto, ferramentas, estado, permissões, ciclos de feedback e uma definição de conclusão.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Na palestra de abertura da QCon San Francisco 2026, Manju Rajashekhar, fundadora e CEO da Mad Labs, defendeu que o harness em torno de um modelo de IA determina o que um agente consegue fazer e com que segurança. A camada organiza o comportamento gerado pelo modelo para torná-lo útil, confiável e repetível.

Rajashekhar comparou essa arquitetura à separação histórica entre aplicativos e sistemas operacionais: os aplicativos definiam comportamentos, enquanto o sistema operacional abstraía o hardware. Como agentes de IA geram comportamento durante a execução, ela argumentou que o software precisa de uma camada própria para organizar esse processo. Em sua formulação, modelo mais harness formam o agente.

It has been revealed that O harness reúne tarefas, contexto, ferramentas, estado, permissões, ciclos de feedback e uma definição de conclusão. O modelo fornece a capacidade; a camada ao redor organiza como ela será aplicada. Por isso, o resultado pode mudar mesmo quando o modelo permanece o mesmo.

In a recent development, O agente mais simples é um modelo executado repetidamente sob controle do harness. Rajashekhar destacou quatro componentes que tornam cada etapa útil. O contexto funciona como memória virtual: a camada reúne o que o modelo precisa para decidir, respeitando o limite da janela de contexto. A recomendação é fornecer uma referência ao material necessário, em vez de despejar todo o conteúdo.

Sources indicate that A interface oferecida ao agente também limita sua capacidade efetiva. Rajashekhar citou um estudo do SWE-agent em que o GPT-4 Turbo resolveu 11,0% dos problemas do SWE-bench Lite usando um terminal simples e 18,0% com uma interface projetada para agentes.

It has been revealed that na execução, o harness funciona como um sistema de processos e permissões, impondo limites por meio de isolamento e credenciais restritas. Um agente de testes, por exemplo, pode receber acesso a uma base de dados de teste sem alcançar a produção. A palestra resumiu a distinção: instruções orientam; limites técnicos impõem as regras.

Industry observers note that O feedback funciona como códigos de retorno: o sistema precisa distinguir entre testes que falharam, testes que não puderam ser executados e resultados desconhecidos. Sem essa separação, o modelo precisa adivinhar o que ocorreu. Em uma tarefa de 20 etapas, com 95% de chance de acerto em cada uma, a chance de concluir tudo corretamente é 36%; detectar 80% dos erros eleva o resultado a 82%.

Quando um agente entra em ciclos improdutivos, a primeira reação costuma ser trocar o modelo. Rajashekhar propôs testar uma mudança no harness antes disso. A ficha do DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash citada na palestra registra resultados entre 65,5% e 74,2% no DeepSWE com o mesmo modelo avaliado em oito harnesses diferentes. As configurações mínimas tiveram os melhores resultados.

Recent findings suggest that em outro estudo, o Qwen3.8-27B resolveu 66,8% de 100 problemas difíceis do LiveCodeBench com uma única chamada. Em uma estrutura com agente gerente, agentes trabalhadores e um registro compartilhado, a taxa chegou a 92,4%. Os exemplos mostram como o desenho da execução pode influenciar o desempenho.

A camada de controle também define o que o agente pode afetar. Rajashekhar contrastou um agente que corrige testes com outro que os apaga para fazê-los passar: a diferença está na autoridade concedida, não na habilidade. Ela citou um incidente de julho de 2026 em que agentes de avaliação da OpenAI, durante um benchmark de captura da bandeira, alcançaram a internet por uma área isolada de código aberta. Segundo o relato, eles tiveram acesso administrativo a clusters internos da Hugging Face por cerca de dois dias e meio.

Rajashekhar também questionou o uso de aprovações humanas como principal barreira. Ao citar o modo automático do Claude Code, observou que as pessoas aprovam a maioria dos pedidos de permissão, o que pode tornar a revisão ineficaz quando há fadiga.

Sources indicate that as premissas incorporadas ao harness envelhecem conforme os modelos melhoram. Sistemas da Anthropic para aplicações de longa duração precisavam reiniciar o contexto quando o Claude Sonnet 4.5 se aproximava do limite; esse comportamento diminuiu com o Opus 4.5. Em sentido inverso, a LangChain moveu para o harness verificações que o modelo ignorava e elevou o GPT-5.2-Codex de 52,8% para 66,5% no Terminal-Bench 2.0, sem trocar o modelo.

It has been revealed that em uma palestra anterior, na QCon AI Boston 2026, Rajashekhar descreveu agentes em produção como sistemas distribuídos e propôs o modelo de atores como ambiente de execução. Nesse desenho, cada tarefa de agente mantém seu estado, recebe eventos por uma caixa de mensagens, registra mudanças em armazenamento durável e opera sob supervisão.

Ao encerrar, ela sugeriu que desenvolvedores examinem as instruções e ferramentas de um agente já em uso, alterem um componente do ciclo em uma tarefa problemática e repitam uma tarefa que já funcionava. O InfoQ publicou a cobertura da palestra.

Confira mais em: https://guiadeti.com.br/noticias/harness-capacidade-seguranca-agentes-ia/.

Does Fluoride In Drinking Water Affect Intelligence? What The Evidence Reveals

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that could childhood exposure to fluoridated water leave a lasting mark on cognition?
  • Could childhood exposure to fluoridated water leave a lasting mark on cognition?
  • Fluoride in community drinking water is not linked to lower adolescent IQ or poorer thinking skills later in life, a long-running US study finds.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that could childhood exposure to fluoridated water leave a lasting mark on cognition? Decades of data offer clues.

Could childhood exposure to fluoridated water leave a lasting mark on cognition? Decades of data offer clues.

Fluoride in community drinking water is not linked to lower adolescent IQ or poorer thinking skills later in life, a long-running US study finds.

Researchers followed a generation of Wisconsin school-leavers, examining cognitive performance from adolescence into their eighties.

Those exposed to fluoridated water did not show a consistent disadvantage compared with people whose communities had no fluoridation.

The findings address concerns that adding fluoride to drinking water to prevent tooth decay could undermine intellectual development.

Professor John Robert Warren, the study’s first author, remarked:.

“Utah, Florida and many municipalities have chosen to remove fluoride from drinking water based on flawed studies that considered the IQ effects of exposure to massive doses of fluoride.

It has been revealed that because levels of fluoride added to municipal drinking water in the U.S. are so much lower, almost all prior evidence from those international studies is not relevant to U.S. public policy debates.”.

The research draws on the Wisconsin Longitudinal Study, which began with over 10,000 people who graduated from high school in 1957.

Researchers combined school IQ records with historical information about community water fluoridation and naturally occurring fluoride levels.

Following participants into old age allowed researchers to examine whether childhood exposure was associated with lasting differences in cognitive performance.

Comparing communities requires care because their residents can differ in ways that also relate to cognitive performance.

Once those background differences were taken into account, there was no consistent evidence that exposure was associated with either better or worse performance.

The same broad pattern appeared when researchers focused on people who had lived in the same county since early childhood, increasing confidence in their estimates of exposure.

Overall, the findings suggest that growing up with fluoridated community water is not associated with poorer cognitive performance in old age.

The study was published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (Warren et al., 2026).

Psychologist, Jeremy Dean, PhD is the founder and author of PsyBlog. He holds a doctorate in psychology from University College London and two other advanced degrees in psychology. He has been writing about scientific research on PsyBlog since 2004. View all posts by Dr Jeremy Dean.

#126290. 8 Trader Joe's Cheeses To Try And 4 To Skip

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2453 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Foodrepublic ↗ Open Full Page

8 Trader Joe's Cheeses To Try And 4 To Skip

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2453 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foodrepublic

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • There's nothing like going to Trader Joe's before hosting a party and stocking up on cool and unusual cheeses.
  • Industry observers note that none of the cheeses I tried were bad, some just weren't worth it for one reason or another, at a time when we're all watching our budgets extra closely.
  • Sources indicate that cranberry Chèvre Goat Cheese is not the only fruit studded fresh goat cheese at Trader Joe's, but it was the first one the store introduced, and it persists for good reason!
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There's nothing like going to Trader Joe's before hosting a party and stocking up on cool and unusual cheeses. It's the perfect time to try something latest or introduce your loved ones to one of your long-standing favorites. Trader Joe's has dozens of cheese at any given time and it can be a little intimidating to narrow down the options. To help out, I sampled some Trader Joe's cheeses to determine which you absolutely need to try, and which you're safe to skip.

Industry observers note that none of the cheeses I tried were bad, some just weren't worth it for one reason or another, at a time when we're all watching our budgets extra closely. As touted in Trader Joe's incredibly easy return policy, every single product has been tried (and loved) by a tech giant representative, so the chances of ending up with something that's objectively bad are pretty slim. Still, there were eight truly standout cheeses among my sampling, and four that you can take a pass on. Prices may vary based on your location.

Sources indicate that cranberry Chèvre Goat Cheese is not the only fruit studded fresh goat cheese at Trader Joe's, but it was the first one the store introduced, and it persists for good reason! Despite its simple composition (a log of fresh goat cheese rolled in sweetened dried cranberries), it is surprisingly complex. It's creamy, tart, and sweet all at once, and the chewy cranberry pieces keep it texturally interesting. It adds a freshness that can help cut through the other heavy, rich options on your cheeseboard, and it's also super versatile.

According to recent reports, if cranberry sauce isn't your preferred vessel for the fruit at the holidays, use this cheese in place of Trader Joe's equally delicious blueberry vanilla goat cheese to make a two-ingredient appetizer with puff pastry sheets. Or, serve the Cranberry Chèvre Goat Cheese with dinner and let your guests slather it on their rolls, instead. Perhaps the most inspired option is using the seasonally perfect fresh goat cheese as a spread for your Thanksgiving leftovers sandwich to take it to a whole newly introduced level.

Trader Joe's Comté Cheese is the kind of cheese you could expect to find at specialty cheese shop, and probably for a lot more money. That is, in part, because all Comté cheese is subject to Appellation d'Origine Protégée (AOP), which are rules that dictate how and where it is made.

Sources indicate that the AOP stamp on Trader Joe's Comté is how you know it's the real deal and follows those same regulations. It's made in just one Alpine region of France (in one of about 134 small villages) using raw milk from one of only two specific breeds of cow, and it is aged for at least four months. The result is a Comté that is firm but creamy, with a somewhat intense smell and a delicately funky flavor. It's definitely one to try, but serve it at room temperature as intended to experience the unique aroma and taste of this strictly-regulated cheese.

Whether or not you have specifically heard of Emmentaler (also called Emmental) cheese, chances are pretty good that you have eaten it. It is the quintessential Swiss cheese that most Americans think of when they hear the term, though there are actually several Swiss cheese varieties.

It has been revealed that trader Joe's Emmentaler has a mild, somewhat sweet and nutty flavor that would be delicious on a ham and Swiss sandwich with Dijon mustard. Emmentaler is even the ultimate fondue cheese. So why is it a skip this time? It does not offer much to set it apart from a Swiss cheese you could buy at any other grocery store. Instead, spend your hard earned money on one of the other kinds of cheese that you can only find exclusively at Trader Joe's. Because, trust us, there are a lot of unique kinds to try at TJ's you can't get anywhere else.

Sources indicate that despite the fact that this Trader Joe's cheese is literally called Unexpected Cheddar Cheese, I'd never tried it, thinking it was just like any other aged cheddar I could buy. I was very wrong (and have since learned my lesson on believing TJ's packaging). There's a reason this cheese came in at No. 2 on our Trader Joe's Product Hall of Fame ranking, and if you've never tried it, now's really the time.

Sources indicate that this cheddar has a really nice nuttiness along with its sharp flavor. It is harder and a bit crumblier than many cheddar cheeses, and has those distinctive crunchy crystals typically found more often in varieties like aged Parmigiano-Reggiano. Those crystals are formed during the aging of certain kinds of cheeses, especially in Italy, and are part of what makes Trader Joe's Unexpected Cheddar so delectable. The crumbly texture might not make it the best cheese for slicing up for sandwiches, but you'll enjoy it a hundred different other ways before it even occurs to you to care about that.

It has been revealed that trader Joe's Cheddar Cheese with Caramelized Onions has been my go-to cheese purchase for over a decade, and, all these years later, it still stands up. It has a softer texture than the store's Unexpected Cheddar, so it slices and melts it a bit more easily, but the caramelized onion flavor is where this cheese really shines. There's nothing else like it.

According to recent reports, it isn't just onions and cheese, either. The flavor is accomplished by blending a caramelized onion marmalade with an English cheddar cheese. The marmalade has a depth of flavor thanks to cider vinegar, red currant juice, lemon juice, olive oil, clove, cinnamon, and ginger. The warm sweetness of the caramelized onion marmalade is expertly balanced with the salty umami flavor of the cheddar itself, and the little bits of onion throughout make it visually and texturally interesting. This is the ideal cheese to bring to a book club meeting (trust me) and goes well with virtually everything.

The double bottles of bubbly being popped open on the front of this cheese's packaging had me hoping for something celebration worthy, but Trader Joe's English Cheddar Cheese with Champagne just isn't it. It's a perfectly fine cheddar cheese, if a bit on the extra salty side, but I had to really concentrate to pick up on any flavor notes that indicated the presence of Champagne.

In a recent development, according to the ingredients, this cheese includes actual Champagne, as well as Marc de Champagne brandy, which is made by distilling all the parts of the grapes that are leftover after being pressed for Champagne. Still, I had to really search for anything I might call Champagne flavor, which was a letdown. At the end of the day, it just wasn't as delicious as the Unexpected Cheddar or the variety with caramelized onions, despite being the most expensive of the bunch at $12.99 per pound.

I don't think I've ever had a bad Brie, but I can confidently say that I've never had a Brie more delicious than Trader Joe's Triple Cream Brie with Wild Mushrooms. Admittedly, I'm a big fan of mushrooms already, but I'm so used to having Brie with jammy fruits that it never occurred to me that the cheese would really shine when paired with the earthy flavors of wild mushrooms.

Served at room temperature with crackers or crusty bread, it spreads like a dream and needs absolutely nothing to improve it. That mentioned, there's nothing like a baked Brie to make a gathering feel like a party and this wild mushroom variety is no exception. If you're short on time, use your microwave to make a "baked" Brie. You'll still get the delicious, gooey texture everyone loves in baked Brie.

Something I didn't learn until I was in my late 20s is that not everyone eats the rind on Brie, despite the fact that it's completely edible (and delicious). If you're not a fan of the earthy rind, you're probably not going to be a fan of the earthy mushrooms in this cheese, either, but I hope you'll give it a chance.

Recent findings suggest that trader Joe's Huntsman Cheese looks very different from other options in the cheese case, with its defined white and orange striped layers. Those different stripes are actually two iconic British cheeses: double Gloucester and Blue Stilton.

The two cheeses work together beautifully. The double Gloucester has a smooth flavor with a somewhat firm texture, while the Blue Stilton, which has a Protected Designation of Origin, is sharp and a bit more crumbly (though it's also creamy at room temperature). While the streaks in the Blue Stilton are indeed mold, it's totally scientifically safe to eat the mold in blue cheese.

It has been revealed that what I love most about this cheese, other than its very unique appearance that makes it perfect for entertaining, is that its a great introduction to blue cheese for people who are leery of its strong flavor. By pairing the Blue Stilton with the double Gloucester, the flavors are well-balanced while still being complex and delicious. Lure your guests in with the striking appearance and amazing flavor of the Huntsman Cheese, then hit them with the Grand Blue (more on that beauty shortly).

Recent findings suggest that I really wanted to love Trader Joe's Pink Peppercorn Fontina Cheese. It's very eye-catching with its vibrant pink coating and I'd incorrectly assumed that pink peppercorns meant it would be a spicy addition to my cheese selection. Avoid making the same mistake I did and take a minute to learn all about the different kinds of peppercorns, including the fact that pink peppercorns aren't true peppercorns and are more closely related to cashews than black peppercorns.

Still, the company's description of the cheese suggests a level of spice that just wasn't there. Instead, the cheese had an almost sweet vegetal flavor. A closer inspection of the ingredients revealed that the peppercorn seasoning blend also includes freeze dried strawberries, strawberry powder, and dehydrated red bell pepper, which made sense in hindsight. The flavors ended up tasting a bit muddled, though the cheese has some promise if it were paired with the right cracker, fruit, or other accompaniment. While it's certainly pretty, it's not worth the effort to make it truly exceptional.

In a recent development, one of the great things about being someone who is unabashedly a fan of blue cheese is that I never feel bad taking a decent sized serving from a cheese platter at an event. Pair it with a crunchy cracker and some red grapes, and I'm in heaven. But even I didn't know that blue cheese could be as good as Trader Joe's Grand Blue Cheese.

This blue cheese is unbelievably creamy. I would have been hard pressed to crumble it unless it was straight from a very cold refrigerator. At room temperature, it sliced almost like soft butter and spread easily on crackers and bread. This is the blue cheese to serve with a black and blue burger, with the cheese melted on top of the patty, or on a pizza with figs, prosciutto, and a balsamic reduction. It's so creamy that I'd love to try it mixed into mac and cheese, if I can manage to make it last long enough next time I buy it (but the need to eat it straight-up might win out).

Sources indicate that havarti is a creamy Danish cheese that holds up super well to both slicing and melting, which makes it a great addition to recipes and on your cheese board. It has a relatively mild, somewhat sweet flavor that lends well to the addition of herbs, peppers, and spices. Perhaps the most iconic variety is Havarti with dill, and Trader Joe's version is worth adding to your shopping list.

In a recent development, fresh dill is used in a lot of Nordic and Scandinavian cooking, so it makes sense that it's a perfect companion to a Danish cheese like Havarti. Trader Joe's Havarti with dill is absolutely packed with the bright herb. If you're the type of person who loves anything dill pickle flavored, you're going to love this cheese. Add it to anything that could use an herbaceous boost, but I highly recommend pairing it with Trader Joe's Unexpected Cheddar for a grilled cheese sandwich that's out of this world. For a bright crunch that brings out the cheese's sweetness, add some crisp apple slices, too. Thank me later.

In a recent development, prior to trying Trader Joe's Toscano Cheese Dusted With Cinnamon, I'd never actually heard of Toscano cheese. It turns out that that's because it's based on another cheese entirely, with a few notable differences. Interestingly enough, while the retailer carries other cheeses with protected status, its Toscano is an interpretation rather than a faithful rendering of Italian Pecorino Toscano, which has a Protected Designation of Origin (PDO).

Italian Pecorino Toscano is a sheep's milk cheese made primarily in Tuscany, while Trader Joe's Toscano (both this cinnamon dusted version and other varieties it offers) are made from cow's milk in Wisconsin. There's nothing inherently wrong with either of those characteristics, and the cinnamon dusting on the cheese gives it a pleasantly warm sweetness, but it feels a bit like a bait and switch. The retailer describes the cheese as being like cheddar in texture and Parmesan in flavor, but I found that it was kind of bland compared to other options, and not even the dusting of cinnamon made it worth the buy.

Recent findings suggest that to ensure a wide range of Trader Joe's cheese, I gathered varieties from all around the world and across many cheese-making styles. While I would happily sample every variety Trader Joe's has to offer, I stuck to a budget of $75, which still allowed me to splurge on a few options and sample a total of 12 cheeses.

It has been revealed that each cheese was tried  first on its own to allow its natural flavor profile a chance to shine. Initial impressions were gathered based on how much I enjoyed the cheese, how much of it I wanted to keep eating, and whether it felt worth it for the cost. That last criterion included considerations like whether the cheese was memorable and how excited I would be to introduce it to a friend. The following day, I prepared a cheese board with all of the cheese samples, two types of crackers, and warm toasted baguette, which I enjoyed with my husband while watching television to solidify my recommendations.
